name: Subway Surfers
summary: Subway Surfers is an endless runner where the player's character sprints away from a pursuing figure while collecting coins, ending each run only when caught. A score multiplier, raised by completing sets of missions, is the game's one long-term progression number, scaling every run's score and gating further content. Two currencies, coins and keys, fund an extensive catalogue of characters, boards and boosts, and a rewarded ad substitutes for a coin or key price at nearly every point in the game. A separate paid product, ad tickets, lets a player buy the same rewards an ad would pay without watching one.
teaser: Subway Surfers offers a rewarded ad as a substitute for nearly every currency price in the game, then sells tickets that buy the same rewards without watching one.

observations.name: Age entry at launch
observations.observed: While Subway Surfers loads, the first thing it asks for is the player's age, set with a slider and then confirmed.

observations.name: Tracking permission
observations.observed: After the age is confirmed, Subway Surfers asks whether it can track the player across other apps and websites. This request comes second, directly after age entry and before anything else.

observations.name: Straight into play
observations.observed: The first screen after these prompts is a Tap to play screen, and tapping it puts the player straight into a run with no menu, account creation or home screen in between.

observations.name: Guided first run
observations.observed: During the first run, Subway Surfers shows arrows for the moves available and introduces new moves as they come up. It prompts a double tap for the hoverboard, and the hoverboard activates as soon as it's used. This guidance runs inside the run itself rather than on a separate tutorial screen, and the hoverboard is introduced here before any store or balance for it is shown.

observations.name: The run
observations.observed: The run is Subway Surfers' core activity: the character runs while being chased, collecting coins and other items until it's caught, at which point the run ends and the player returns to the home screen. Coins collected during the run add to a balance shown on the home screen, 676 coins after a first run, and the run also produces a score shown alongside that balance. Subway Surfers offers no continuation, revive or retry option at the moment of being caught, and no energy, lives, tickets or other limit on how often a run can be started.

observations.name: Home screen hub
observations.observed: Between runs, the player is on a home screen that shows the score and coin balance and carries a set of offers and entry points. Four navigation buttons sit at the top, Missions, Me, Shop and Events, and the home screen also features a Daily Login button, a What's New button, a Top Run button, the Coins Galore offer and the Bonus Keys Trail offer, along with a prompt to add friends and compete for the highest score to get rewards. Events is locked. What the What's New button shows isn't stated.

observations.name: Collecting letters
observations.observed: Partway through a run, the player begins collecting letters that change along with the day of the week. What the letters spell, what completing the set unlocks, and what it pays aren't stated.

observations.name: Missions
observations.observed: Missions open a panel that explains finishing missions raises the score multiplier, and a higher multiplier means a higher score. The current mission set holds three missions: pick up 100 coins in one run, jump 15 times, and pick up two pogo sticks. Each mission can be completed by playing, and Subway Surfers also offers to complete one immediately, for 1,700 coins on the coin and pogo-stick missions, or by watching an ad on the jump mission. The missions panel shows the player's current score multiplier, and missions are shown as a set of three together. Whether missions refresh on a schedule, and what replaces a completed one, aren't stated.

observations.name: Boosters and head starts
observations.observed: The Boosts tab offers a score booster, usable up to three times to raise the multiplier by five, six or seven for one run, priced at 3,000 coins or one ad. Score boosters raise the multiplier for one run only, without changing its standing value.

observations.name: Permanent upgrades
observations.observed: The Upgrades tab under Me offers upgrades that permanently increase the duration of pickups: the Jetpack, which flies into the sky to collect bonus coins; Super Sneakers, which jump higher than normal; Coin Magnet, which automatically collects nearby coins; and a 2x Multiplier, which doubles the score while it's active. Each costs 500 coins. These are pickups collected inside runs, distinct from the items held and applied from the Boosts tab. How many upgrade steps exist per power-up, and whether the price rises per step, aren't stated.

observations.observed: Coins are collected in runs and held as a balance on the home screen. They're spent on hoverboards (300), head starts (2,000), score boosters (3,000), each upgrade (500), the mystery box (500), completing a mission immediately (1,700), and on characters, boards and flash-deal items, and they're also sold for money. The Coin Magnet and Jetpack upgrades are both framed around collecting more coins.

observations.name: Keys
observations.observed: Keys are a second currency, shown at the top of the screen. They're gained by watching rewarded ads, including a banner offer of three keys for a video and a store offer of three blue keys, and they're sold for money. Keys are spent on characters (459 keys for one), on flash-deal items, and on recovering a missed login reward (5 keys). Keys are also included inside paid offers, among them 15 keys in the No More Forced Ads offer and the Bonus Keys Trail. Subway Surfers refers to "blue keys" in some places; whether these are the same currency as keys isn't stated, since the currency bar lists only keys, coins and hoverboards. A line about opening the token box with keys by watching a video doesn't fully hold together, and it does not make clear how keys and the token box relate.

systemView: Subway Surfers is a complex system. Its spine is the score multiplier: missions raise it, it's the number that scales every run's score, and it's what Quests, Collections and a bundled purchase all key off. Ads run across that spine as connective tissue rather than a layer of their own, substituting for currency at boosts, missions, the post-run prize and missed login days alike, with ad tickets and several limited offers sold specifically against that same ad layer.

mechanicWriteups.name: Rewarded Advertisement
mechanicWriteups.summary: A rewarded ad substitutes for a coin or key price at nearly every spending point in the game, and a separate paid product exists to skip watching them.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Ads pay out across a wide range of surfaces: coins (500, 300), keys (three keys, three blue keys), a hoverboard, each boost, an increase of the post-run prize from 1,000 to 2,000 coins, completion of a mission, recovery of a missed login day, and slots inside the Daily Rewards and Coins Galore offers. Two offers, Mystery Box Mania and Coins Galore, make one reward conditional on several ads watched, tracked by a counter. Subway Surfers also sells ad tickets, which buy the same rewards an ad would pay without watching one.
mechanicWriteups.presented: An ad option sits beside the coin or key price at nearly every place Subway Surfers asks for one, so the two routes read as equally valid choices rather than one being a fallback. The Daily Rewards screen is built entirely around five ad-watch slots. Mystery Box Mania's counter adds together ads watched anywhere in the game toward one reward, and Coins Galore runs the same pattern against a countdown.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Selling ad tickets is the least usual part of this: it turns the habit of watching ads for a reward into something a player can buy their way out of while keeping the reward, rather than the more common choice of just removing the ads outright. Letting an ad complete a mission, not just discount it, is also a stronger substitute for play than a coin price achieves on its own.
findings: An ad substitutes for a coin or key price on boosts, hoverboards, missed login days, and one mission.
Watching an ad can raise the post-run prize from 1,000 to 2,000 coins.
Two counters, Mystery Box Mania and Coins Galore, bank multiple ad watches toward one larger reward.
Ad tickets are sold as a way to receive the same rewards without watching anything.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the Daily Rewards screen with its five ad-watch slots; the Coins Galore offer with its ad counter and countdown; the ad ticket pricing screen.

mechanicWriteups.name: Boosters
mechanicWriteups.summary: A held count of hoverboards plus two named, coin-or-ad-priced boosts, each usable up to three times, apply their effect only for the run ahead.
mechanicWriteups.observed: A hoverboard is activated in a run with a double tap and protects the character from crashing for 30 seconds; Subway Surfers holds a count of them, and more can be had one at a time by watching an ad or bought for 300 coins each. A score booster raises the multiplier by five, six or seven for one run, and a head start begins a run already at higher speed; both are usable up to three times per run, priced at 3,000 and 2,000 coins respectively, or one ad each.
mechanicWriteups.presented: All three sit together on a Boosts tab, which states that boosts can only be used once and are worth stocking up on ahead of time. The same single ad buys any of the three regardless of their very different coin prices.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Pricing a hoverboard, a head start and a score booster at one flat ad each, while their coin prices span a tenfold range, makes the ad route the better deal for the two more expensive boosts, at least in time rather than money.
findings: Boosts are used up per run, not held as a permanent upgrade.
A score booster and a head start can each be applied up to three times in a single run.
The same single ad buys a hoverboard, a head start or a score booster despite a tenfold difference in their coin prices.
Boosts are also included in paid bundles in quantities of 10 or 20.

mechanicWriteups.name: Soft Currency
mechanicWriteups.summary: Coins are earned from nearly a dozen separate sources and spent across almost every system in the game, with keys sharing the same earn-through-play path via ads.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Coins are collected in runs and added to a balance, and are also paid by the post-run prize, ad offers, the Coins Galore offer, adding a friend, missed login rewards and achievements. They're spent on hoverboards, boosts, upgrades, the mystery box, completing a mission immediately, and on characters and boards. Keys are gained by watching ads repeatedly and spent on characters, flash-deal items and recovering a missed login day.
mechanicWriteups.presented: Coins sit as a running balance on the home screen from the first run onward, visible everywhere a price is shown. Keys sit beside them in the same currency bar, with their own ad-watch entry points spread across the home screen and the store.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Coins have no single dominant source. Runs, ads, offers, a social action and a return mechanic all pay into the same balance, so no one habit is required to keep it funded.
findings: Coins are earned through play, through ads, through a social action, and through returning daily.
Keys are earned only through watching ads, with no coin-to-key conversion shown.
Both currencies fund overlapping purchases: boosts, characters, and boards can be bought with either.
Adding a friend pays 5,000 coins directly into this same balance.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the home screen showing the coin balance and score together after a run.

mechanicWriteups.name: Hard Currency
mechanicWriteups.summary: Coins, keys and ad tickets are all sold directly for money in packs, with ad tickets sold specifically to buy out the ad-for-reward exchange.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Coins are sold from 7.5 thousand for $0.99 up to 1.25 million for $99.99, and keys from 25 for $4.99 up to 800 for $99.99. Ad tickets are sold in packs of 10, 25 and 60, and bundled into several limited offers alongside boards and boosts.
mechanicWriteups.presented: Coin and key packs sit together in the store at a range of price points, buyable in any order with no unlocking sequence between them. Ad tickets and the offers built around them sit at the very top of the store, ahead of the currency packs.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Selling ad tickets makes the ad layer itself a second thing to buy, distinct from paying for what the ads would have granted. A player can pay to stop watching ads and still receive what watching them would have paid out.
findings: Coins and keys are both sold directly for money in packs, with no conversion step between them.
Ad tickets are sold in packs of 10, 25 and 60, and are bundled into several limited-time offers.
Ad ticket and currency offers sit at the top of the store, ahead of the currency packs themselves.
No free way to get an ad ticket is shown.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the coin and key pack pricing screen; the ad ticket pack pricing screen.

mechanicWriteups.name: Daily Login Rewards
mechanicWriteups.summary: A 20-login calendar pays a hoverboard on completion, and any missed day stays claimable afterward for keys or an ad rather than being lost.
mechanicWriteups.observed: A Daily Login surface appears on opening the app, stating that checking in daily pays rewards and that missed days can be caught up on. It counts toward 20 logins, after which the Freebird hoverboard is paid, and a missed day carries its own catch-up option, claimable for five keys or one ad.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The calendar pops up on open and sits alongside a Daily Login button on the home screen. A missed day shows its own marker rather than breaking the sequence, and tapping it opens the five-keys-or-an-ad choice directly.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Making every missed day recoverable removes the usual penalty for missing a day, while still keeping a reason to come back: the 20-login target and its hoverboard reward stay reachable either way, just more slowly without the ad or the keys.
findings: Twenty logins pay the Freebird hoverboard, also shown as a locked reward in the board catalogue.
A missed day is not lost; it stays claimable for five keys or one ad.
The reward for each individual day besides the 20-login hoverboard is not named.
The calendar sits separately from the five-slot, fully ad-based Daily Rewards track.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the Daily Login calendar with the Freebird hoverboard reward and a missed-day catch-up marker visible.

mechanicWriteups.name: Daily Claim Pack
mechanicWriteups.summary: One $7.99 purchase on day one unlocks nine further days of free keys, a purchase that pays out in daily installments rather than all at once.
mechanicWriteups.observed: The Bonus Keys Trail offer pays 40 keys for a $7.99 purchase on its first day, then releases free keys on each of the following nine days, in amounts of 20, 5, 10, 20, 10, 55, 10, 10 and 20. The offer is shown on the home screen with a limited window to take it.
mechanicWriteups.presented: All nine free days are shown up front, before the purchase, so the full ten-day payout is visible before committing.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Spreading a single purchase's payout over ten days turns one transaction into ten separate reasons to come back, in a way a lump-sum reward wouldn't.
findings: One $7.99 purchase on day one unlocks nine further days of free keys.
The nine free days total 160 keys beyond the 40 paid for directly.
All ten days' amounts are shown before the purchase is made.
Whether each day must be actively claimed, and what happens to an unclaimed day, isn't stated.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the Bonus Keys Trail offer showing the day-one purchase price and the following nine days' amounts.

mechanicWriteups.name: Leveling
mechanicWriteups.summary: A permanent score multiplier rises only through completing mission sets, and directly scales the score every run afterward pays out.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Subway Surfers keeps a score multiplier that rises as mission sets are completed and that scales the score a run produces. Its states are referred to as levels, and a paid bundle can add five levels to it at once. The multiplier's current value shows inside the missions panel.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The missions panel opens by explaining the connection directly: finishing missions raises the multiplier, and a higher multiplier means a higher score. The multiplier doesn't have its own dedicated screen outside that panel.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Tying the score multiplier only to mission completion, with no separate experience points or activity counter behind it, makes missions the sole route to the game's one long-term progression number, whether reached by playing, paying coins, watching an ad, or buying the multiplier bundle directly.
findings: The score multiplier rises only through completing sets of missions.
The multiplier permanently scales the score a run produces.
A $4.99 bundle adds five multiplier levels at once, alongside coins and keys.
How many missions are needed per level isn't stated.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the missions panel showing the current multiplier value and the mission set beneath it.

mechanicWriteups.name: Progression Gate
mechanicWriteups.summary: Four separate surfaces, Quests, Collections, the Freebird board and Events, each stay locked behind their own named threshold on the score multiplier or the login count.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Quests stays locked until score multiplier 4, and Collections until score multiplier 7, each stating its requirement on the locked surface itself. The Freebird board stays locked until 20 logins. Events stays locked until a threshold described as four stars, level 4.
mechanicWriteups.presented: Each locked surface can still be opened and states its own requirement plainly, rather than hiding behind a generic locked label. The Quests and Collections surfaces also carry the score multiplier bundle, offering a paid route past the same number gating them.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Every named gate here reads its requirement off a number the player is already earning through ordinary play, the score multiplier or the login count, rather than introducing a separate currency or task just to unlock content.
findings: Quests unlocks at score multiplier 4 and Collections at score multiplier 7.
The Freebird board unlocks at 20 logins.
Events unlocks at a threshold described as four stars, level 4, without saying which measure that is.
The score multiplier bundle is offered directly on the locked Quests and Collections surfaces.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the locked Quests and Collections surfaces showing their stated multiplier requirements and the bundle offered on each.

mechanicWriteups.name: Leaderboard
mechanicWriteups.summary: A weekly Top Run ranks the player against friends and their country, but only once a 25,000-point entry score has been reached.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Top Run frames itself as competing against friends and foes to climb ranks and earn medals, with a new chance to compete every week. It shows the player's standing against other players in their country and against their friends, and requires a score of at least 25,000 to enter the current week.
mechanicWriteups.presented: Top Run is reached from its own home-screen button, separate from the missions and score-multiplier surfaces that feed the score it ranks.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Setting a minimum score to even enter turns Top Run into a competition among players who've already cleared a bar, rather than an open ranking anyone can join and climb from zero.
findings: Entry to the current week's Top Run requires a score of at least 25,000.
Two views are shown: standing against friends and standing against other players in the same country.
The competition resets weekly, with a new chance to compete each week.
Where the player's own row sits within either list isn't stated.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the Top Run screen showing the country standings, the weekly reset, and the 25,000 entry score.

mechanicWriteups.name: Achievement
mechanicWriteups.summary: A named Achievements list pays out in-game currency on the criteria it lists, separate from the score multiplier that otherwise tracks progress.
mechanicWriteups.observed: An Achievements surface lists a set of achievements and what each one pays once attained, with some of that reward paid in in-game currency.
mechanicWriteups.presented: Achievements are reached from the home screen's navigation, apart from the missions and multiplier surfaces that drive most of the game's other progression.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Keeping achievements as their own list, separate from the score multiplier, gives Subway Surfers two different progress records running side by side rather than folding recognition into the same number missions already raise.
findings: Achievements are listed with what each one pays.
At least some achievement rewards are paid in in-game currency.
The specific criteria for individual achievements aren't named.
Whether an achieved reward is claimed or granted automatically isn't stated.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the Achievements list showing an entry and its stated reward.

mechanicWriteups.name: Reward Multiplier
mechanicWriteups.summary: Watching one ad turns the standard 1,000-coin post-run prize into 2,000 coins, offered at the very moment that prize is first shown.
mechanicWriteups.observed: On returning to the home screen after a run, Subway Surfers shows a prize worth 1,000 coins, then offers to raise it to 2,000 coins for watching an ad.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The offer sits directly on the same prize screen, immediately after a run ends, before the player has seen anything else on the home screen.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Placing this offer at the very first moment after a run, ahead of every other surface on the home screen, makes it the highest-traffic point at which Subway Surfers asks for an ad.
findings: The post-run prize is 1,000 coins before any ad is watched.
Watching one ad raises it to 2,000 coins.
The offer appears immediately on returning to the home screen, before any other surface.
Whether 2,000 is the full new total or added on top of the 1,000 isn't stated.

sectionLeadIns.onboarding: Subway Surfers asks for an age and a tracking permission before anything else, then puts the player straight into a guided first run with no menu in between.
sectionLeadIns.core-loop: Subway Surfers' core loop is a run through the subway, ended by being caught, between which the player manages a home screen full of missions, boosts and offers. The score multiplier, raised by completing missions, is the throughline connecting the run to everything else in the game.
sectionLeadIns.goals: The score multiplier is Subway Surfers' one long-term number, raised by missions and read by several of the game's other surfaces. Alongside it sit a permanent set of upgrades, a named achievements list, and characters unlocked by collecting items during runs.
sectionLeadIns.access: Four surfaces in Subway Surfers stay locked behind a stated threshold: Quests, Collections, the Freebird board, and Events. Each names its own requirement, and some characters carry their own separate conditions.
sectionLeadIns.economy: Subway Surfers runs on two spendable currencies, coins and keys, alongside a separate ad-ticket product and an event-specific currency. Ads sit beside nearly every price in this section as a free alternative to spending either currency.
sectionLeadIns.social: Subway Surfers' social surfaces are thin and reward-linked: adding a friend pays a fixed bonus, and a weekly leaderboard compares the player against friends and their country.
sectionLeadIns.reach: Two surfaces in Subway Surfers send something outside the game: a shareable player profile, and a photo studio built around the player's own character.
sectionLeadIns.monetization: Subway Surfers' shop sits behind three tabs, Offers, Store and Boosts, with ad-related offers given the store's leading position ahead of the currency packs themselves.
sectionLeadIns.returns: Four separate surfaces greet the player on opening Subway Surfers: a login calendar, a fully ad-based rewards track, a timed currency offer, and a daily gift in the store.

system.tagline: A score-multiplier progression spine with a rewarded ad substituting for currency at nearly every point along it.
system.overview: Subway Surfers is a complex system built around a score multiplier that missions raise and that scales every run's score, gating Quests, Collections and a bundled purchase as it climbs. Ads run across that spine as connective tissue rather than a layer of their own, substituting for a coin or key price on boosts, missions, the post-run prize and missed login days alike. A separate paid product, ad tickets, is sold specifically against that same ad layer, letting a player buy the rewards an ad would pay without watching one.
system.loop: The core loop is: run through the subway, collecting coins, until caught → return to the home screen for a post-run prize, raisable to 2,000 coins for an ad → complete missions by playing, by coins, or by an ad to raise the score multiplier → use coins and keys on boosts, upgrades, characters and boards → check the daily login calendar and the fully ad-based Daily Rewards track → spend the score multiplier's climb to clear the Quests and Collections gates, or buy past them with a bundle. Ads substitute for currency at nearly every one of these steps.
system.keyInsight: Ads are the connective tissue here, not a layer of their own: the same rewarded ad substitutes for a coin price on a boost, buys out a mission, recovers a missed login day, and doubles the post-run prize, all at the flattest possible cost regardless of what the coin price would have been. Selling ad tickets on top of that turns the habit itself into a second product: a player can pay to stop watching ads and still receive what watching them would have paid out.
system.whatMakesItWork: The score multiplier gives ads something to substitute for at every step: missions can be played, bought with coins, or bought with one ad, and all three routes feed the same permanent number. Because the multiplier is the only long-term progression axis and everything else, boosts, the post-run prize, missed login days, reads its price in either coins or one flat ad, the ad layer never feels bolted on. It's priced into the same choices the currency already offers.

roles.role: A rewarded ad substitutes for a coin or key price on boosts, hoverboards, missed login days and one mission, raises the post-run prize from 1,000 to 2,000 coins, and fills the five-slot Daily Rewards track entirely. Ad tickets are sold as a way to receive the same rewards without watching one.
A held count of hoverboards plus a score booster and a head start, each usable up to three times per run, priced at one flat ad or a coin price that varies tenfold across the three.

Coins are earned through play, ads, a social action and daily return, and spent across boosts, upgrades, the mystery box and mission buyouts. Keys share the same ad-earned path and fund characters and missed-day recovery.
Coins, keys and ad tickets are all sold directly for money in packs, with ad tickets and several limited offers sold specifically to buy out the ad-for-reward exchange.
A 20-login calendar pays the Freebird hoverboard on completion, with any missed day staying claimable for five keys or one ad rather than lost.
The Bonus Keys Trail turns one $7.99 purchase on day one into nine further days of free keys, shown in full before the purchase is made.
The score multiplier rises only through completing mission sets and permanently scales the score every run produces afterward.

Quests, Collections, the Freebird board and Events each stay locked behind their own stated threshold on the score multiplier or the login count, with the score-multiplier bundle offered as a paid route past two of them.
A weekly Top Run ranks the player against friends and their country, but only once a 25,000-point entry score, scaled by the multiplier, has been reached.
A named Achievements list pays out in-game currency on its own listed criteria, a separate, much thinner record running alongside the score multiplier.
Watching one ad turns the standard 1,000-coin post-run prize into 2,000 coins, offered at the very first moment the player sees after a run.

connections.title: Ads substitute for coin prices on boosts
connections.desc: The hoverboard, the score booster and the head start can each be bought for coins or for one ad, with the ad price flat across all three despite a tenfold spread in their coin prices.
connections.effect: A player with no coins can still keep every boost stocked, since the ad route never runs dry the way a coin balance can.

connections.title: Coins buy the same boosts at three different prices
connections.desc: The hoverboard costs 300 coins, the head start 2,000, and the score booster 3,000, the same three items the ad route prices flat.
connections.effect: Coins and ads sit side by side as two full-featured routes into the same boosts, not one primary path and a fallback.

connections.title: One ad doubles the post-run prize
connections.desc: The post-run prize pays 1,000 coins, and watching one ad raises it to 2,000, offered at the very first moment on the home screen after a run.
connections.effect: The highest-traffic ad placement in the game sits at the exact moment a player is most engaged, right after finishing a run.

connections.title: An ad can complete a mission outright
connections.desc: The jump-15-times mission can be finished immediately by watching an ad rather than by playing or paying coins, and missions are what raise the score multiplier.
connections.effect: An ad substitutes for actual play, not just for a currency price, on the game's one long-term progression number.

connections.title: The multiplier gates Quests and Collections
connections.desc: Quests unlocks at score multiplier 4 and Collections at score multiplier 7, both stated on their own locked surfaces.
connections.effect: The same number missions raise is what opens two further parts of the game, so progression and access run on one shared measure.

connections.title: The Freebird board sits behind the login count
connections.desc: The Freebird board is locked in the board catalogue behind 20 logins, the same target the Daily Login surface counts toward.
connections.effect: A reward the login calendar promises is also a gate the board catalogue enforces, so the two surfaces state the same requirement from two directions.

connections.title: Ads recover a missed login day
connections.desc: A missed day in the Daily Login sequence carries a catch-up option, claimable for five keys or one ad.
connections.effect: Missing a day carries no hard penalty: the ad route keeps the 20-login target reachable without spending keys.

connections.title: One key purchase seeds ten days of returns
connections.desc: The Bonus Keys Trail's first day is a $7.99 purchase for 40 keys, and free keys follow on each of the next nine days.
connections.effect: A single transaction is stretched into ten separate reasons to open the app, rather than paying out all at once.

connections.title: The multiplier decides who can enter Top Run
connections.desc: Top Run requires a score of at least 25,000 to enter the current week, and the score multiplier is what scales every run's score.
connections.effect: Climbing the score multiplier is a precondition for competing at all, not just an advantage once inside.
